LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Stage Microphone — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the stage microphone — the handheld singer’s mic that tilts, pulls away on the big notes, and comes with its own manners: thank the crowd, share the stage.

What is this?

The stage microphone is the handheld kind singers grab: held at the chin, tilted for high notes, pulled away for the loudest ones so the speakers do not shout. It lives on a stand between songs and waits its turn.

What does it mean?

The stage mic adds performance craft to the microphone’s physics: the PULL-AWAY on big notes (the pro move), the tilt that shapes the sound, and the manners — the mic is shared, the crowd is thanked, the stage is a kind place.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three stage-mic ideas: hold it at the chin, not the lips — singing needs jaw room; PULL it away on the very biggest notes — let the speakers finish the shout; and between songs it rests on the stand — the mic waits its turn like everyone on stage.

Why this matters

Stage craft — where to stand, when to pull, how to thank — is the part of music no textbook teaches late. Playing it at four, with a hairbrush, builds performers who are generous on real stages.

What it teaches

Performance gestures (tilt, pull-away), breath-and-jaw awareness at the chin, turn-taking on stage, and crowd manners — the bow, the thank-you.

Words to learn

stagehandheldchintiltpull awaystandcrowd

Say this to your child

“"The stage mic is the singer’s friend! Hold it at your chin — your jaw needs room to sing. Tilt it a little for the high notes… and on the BIGGEST note of all — pull it away! Let the speakers finish the shout. Then back on the stand it goes, waiting its turn. And at the end: bow, and thank the crowd — that is stage manners."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the stage microphone — the singer’s mic, the one stars grab and tilt."
  2. The chin hold: mic at the CHIN, not squashing the lips — singers need their jaws free to open wide.
  3. The pull-away: on the biggest, loudest note — pull the mic AWAY! The speakers finish the shout. That is the pro move; practise it on one giant note.
  4. The stand rest: between songs the mic goes back on its stand — everyone on stage waits their turn, even the mic.
  5. Play the stage game below and close: "chin, tilt, pull away — and thank the crowd."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Microphone" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a yellow handheld stage microphone illustrated below — exactly as the stage star’s tool looks.

Ask your child

"Where does the stage mic rest — lips or chin? What do we do on the biggest note? Where does the mic wait between songs?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Chin, not lips!" "Pull away on the BIG one!" or the star’s manners: "Thank you, crowd — good night!"

Out in the real world

Stage mics tilt and pull away in every concert film and talent show — watch one chorus closely and catch the pull-away on the high note. The move is everywhere once your eyes know it.

Try it together

The Star’s Set: hairbrush mic, sofa-arm stage. One song — hummed or sung — with the three pro moves: chin hold, tilt on the highs, PULL-AWAY on the giant finish. The crowd (everyone else) goes wild. Then the manners: mic to the stand, bow, "THANK YOU!" — and the next star gets the stage. Everyone performs, everyone claps: that is show business, four years old.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the mic rest while singing? What is the move on the biggest note? What do we do at the end?" At the chin, pull away, bow and thank — three answers and the stage is yours.

Parent tips

The pull-away is the star of the lesson — one giant note, one dramatic pull, guaranteed laughter. And rotate the stage fast: short sets, big applause, generous crowds.

This lesson pairs with the Stage Microphone flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).
